front: A patient with type 1 diabetes is made nil by mouth for surgery at noon. The admission order says to hold all insulin.
bottom: Keep basal insulin. Never stop it in type 1 diabetes.

bullets.clue: Mealtime insulin can be held while the patient is not eating. The background need does not disappear.
bullets.treat: Give most of the basal dose, with dextrose if needed, and check glucose often.
bullets.trap: Holding every insulin because the patient is not eating.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
source.recommendation: Type 1 diabetes still needs basal insulin during fasting. Stopping it produces ketoacidosis.

diagram.alt: Text card. Keep basal insulin. Never stop it in type 1 diabetes.

front: A patient on a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor is booked for elective surgery in two days. The medicine is still on the list for the morning of surgery.
bottom: Stop that medicine three days before surgery.

bullets.clue: Ertugliflozin needs four days. The others need three. The risk is ketoacidosis with a near-normal glucose.
bullets.treat: Hold the drug, operate, and restart when the patient is eating and the acute illness is over.
bullets.trap: Continuing the tablet the morning of surgery because the glucose has been excellent.

source.guideline: FDA safety communication on SGLT2 inhibitors and surgery
source.recommendation: SGLT2 inhibitors are stopped about three days before surgery to reduce euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis.

diagram.alt: Text card. Stop that medicine three days before surgery.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: perioperative care
front: A patient who has never taken a beta blocker is given one for the first time on the morning of major surgery, to make the numbers look calm.
bottom: Do not start a beta blocker on the day of surgery.

bullets.clue: A large perioperative trial showed more stroke and death when blockers were started immediately before surgery.
bullets.treat: Continue a beta blocker the patient already takes. Do not invent a new one on the morning of the operation.
bullets.trap: A new perioperative beta blocker as a routine clearance step.

source.recommendation: Beta blockers already in use are continued. Starting one on the day of surgery causes harm.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not start a beta blocker on the day of surgery.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: perioperative care
front: A patient who can climb a flight of stairs is scheduled for cataract surgery. A preoperative stress test has been ordered to clear them.
bottom: Cancel the stress test. This surgery does not need it.

bullets.clue: Adequate functional capacity and a low-risk operation do not get ischemia testing.
bullets.treat: Proceed. Reserve testing for poor capacity plus a higher-risk operation when the result would change management.
bullets.trap: A stress test before every anesthetic.

source.recommendation: Patients who can climb a flight of stairs and are having low-risk surgery do not need preoperative stress testing.

diagram.alt: Text card. Cancel the stress test. This surgery does not need it.

front: A patient is scheduled for cataract extraction next week and takes aspirin for a prior stent. The eye team asks whether to stop it.
bottom: Continue the aspirin.

bullets.clue: Cataract surgery is very low bleeding risk. A stent is a high clotting risk if both antiplatelet drugs disappear.
bullets.treat: Continue aspirin. Do not stop a P2Y12 inhibitor early after a stent for this operation.
bullets.trap: Holding all blood thinners for a week before a cataract.

source.guideline: ACC/AHA perioperative and dual antiplatelet guidance
source.recommendation: Aspirin is continued for cataract surgery. Dual therapy after a recent stent is not stopped for a low-bleeding-risk procedure.

diagram.alt: Text card. Continue the aspirin.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: medication use
front: A statin is on the list to hold for the week before elective surgery because the family wants fewer pills.
bottom: Continue the statin.

bullets.clue: Perioperative statin withdrawal is not helpful, and continuation is reasonable.
bullets.treat: Take the statin through the surgical window unless there is a separate reason to stop it, such as a high creatine kinase with pain.
bullets.trap: A routine week off the statin before the operating room.

source.recommendation: Statins are continued around noncardiac surgery. They are not a routine hold.

diagram.alt: Text card. Continue the statin.

front: During anesthesia the end-tidal carbon dioxide rises, the jaw is rigid, and the temperature starts to climb after a volatile agent.
bottom: This is malignant hyperthermia. Give dantrolene.

bullets.clue: The trigger is a volatile anesthetic or succinylcholine. The first number to move is often carbon dioxide, not temperature.
bullets.treat: Stop the trigger, hyperventilate with oxygen, and give dantrolene. Call for the cart.
bullets.trap: Assuming a postoperative fever and ordering a culture.

source.guideline: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States
source.recommendation: Malignant hyperthermia is rising carbon dioxide, rigidity, and hyperthermia during anesthesia. Dantrolene is the antidote.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is malignant hyperthermia. Give dantrolene.

front: During a nerve block the patient reports a metallic taste and ringing, then has a seizure.
bottom: Local anesthetic toxicity. Give lipid emulsion.

bullets.clue: Neurologic symptoms come first. Cardiac collapse can follow.
bullets.treat: Stop the injection, support the airway, benzodiazepine for the seizure, and intravenous lipid emulsion.
bullets.trap: Treating the seizure as epilepsy and never naming the anesthetic.

source.guideline: ASRA local anesthetic systemic toxicity checklist
source.recommendation: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity begins with neurologic warning symptoms and is treated with lipid emulsion.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Local anesthetic toxicity. Give lipid emulsion.

front: On the evening of surgery the temperature is 38.0, the incision is dry, the lungs are clear, and the patient is drinking.
bottom: Do not start broad antibiotics for this number.

bullets.clue: A low fever in the first hours is usually inflammatory. Atelectasis is an old explanation and not a reason for a drug.
bullets.treat: Examine the patient. Culture and treat when there is a source or the patient looks ill.
bullets.trap: A sepsis bundle for every first-night temperature of 38.

source.recommendation: Immediate postoperative low-grade fever with a normal exam is observed. Antibiotics follow a source.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not start broad antibiotics for this number.

front: A patient cannot void eight hours after pelvic surgery. The bladder scan shows 700 milliliters. The abdomen is uncomfortable.
bottom: Drain the bladder. Do not give a fluid bolus.

bullets.clue: The bladder is already full. More fluid makes it fuller.
bullets.treat: Catheterize, record the volume, and look for the medicine or the pain that caused the retention.
bullets.trap: A liter of saline for low urine output when the bladder is distended.

source.recommendation: Postoperative urinary retention is diagnosed with a bladder volume and treated by drainage.

diagram.alt: Text card. Drain the bladder. Do not give a fluid bolus.

front: An older adult is suddenly confused on hospital night two. Someone orders a restraint and a benzodiazepine to help them sleep.
bottom: Find the cause of the delirium. Do not lead with a restraint or a benzodiazepine.

bullets.clue: Infection, drugs, urine retention, constipation, pain, and withdrawal are the usual causes.
bullets.treat: Treat the cause, restore sleep and glasses and hearing, and use an antipsychotic only if the patient is in danger.
bullets.trap: A benzodiazepine as a sleeper for new confusion.

source.recommendation: Delirium is a medical emergency of attention. Benzodiazepines worsen it unless the cause is withdrawal.

diagram.alt: Text card. Find the cause of the delirium. Do not lead with a restraint or a benzodiazepine.

front: An 82-year-old has fallen twice. The medicine list includes a nightly benzodiazepine. Blood pressure drops 25 points on standing.
bottom: Stop the sedative and treat the blood pressure drop.

bullets.clue: Falls are usually many small risks added together. A head CT is for a head strike or a blood thinner, not the whole plan.
bullets.treat: Orthostatic vitals, medication review, vision, and strength. Taper the benzodiazepine. Do not stop it tonight.
bullets.trap: A normal head CT and a discharge with the same pill bottle.

source.recommendation: Benzodiazepines and orthostasis are modifiable fall risks. A sudden stop of a chronic benzodiazepine can cause withdrawal.

diagram.alt: Text card. Stop the sedative and treat the blood pressure drop.

front: Constant dribbling, a weak stream, and a post-void residual of 400 milliliters. An anticholinergic is being considered for the wetness.
bottom: This is overflow. An anticholinergic will make it worse.

bullets.clue: Urge incontinence wants the bladder to calm down. Overflow wants the bladder to empty.
bullets.treat: Relieve the obstruction or catheterize. Do not give a bladder-relaxing drug to a bladder that cannot empty.
bullets.trap: Oxybutynin for every wet older man.

source.guideline: AUA male lower urinary tract symptoms guideline
source.recommendation: A high post-void residual means overflow. Antimuscarinic drugs are for urge incontinence and worsen retention.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is overflow. An anticholinergic will make it worse.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: skin and subcutaneous tissue
front: A pressure injury was stage 3. After two weeks of offloading the base is filling with tissue and is now more shallow.
bottom: Do not renumber it as a stage 2.

bullets.clue: Pressure injuries are not reverse-staged as they heal. The original depth stays in the record.
bullets.treat: Keep offloading and nutrition. Describe the healing wound. Do not call it a lower stage.
bullets.trap: Charting stage 2 because the hole looks smaller.

source.recommendation: Pressure injuries are not reverse staged. A healing stage 3 injury remains a healing stage 3.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not renumber it as a stage 2.

front: An 84-year-old with a creatinine of 2.1 has a hot toe. Indomethacin is prescribed for ten days.
bottom: Do not use a full-dose anti-inflammatory in this kidney.

bullets.clue: Older adults with chronic kidney disease bleed and worsen their creatinine on chronic nonsteroidal drugs.
bullets.treat: A short course of a steroid, or a carefully dosed alternative, plus the kidney in view. Not indomethacin.
bullets.trap: A ten-day nonsteroidal drug for gout in chronic kidney disease.

source.recommendation: Chronic or high-dose nonsteroidal drugs are inappropriate in older adults with chronic kidney disease.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not use a full-dose anti-inflammatory in this kidney.

front: A patient with advanced dementia has recurrent aspiration and is losing weight. The family asks for a permanent feeding tube so the pneumonias will stop.
bottom: A tube does not stop aspiration and does not lengthen life here.

bullets.clue: Careful hand feeding is the option that matches the evidence in advanced dementia.
bullets.treat: Explain the limit of the tube, treat comfort, and offer assisted oral feeding.
bullets.trap: A percutaneous tube as the way to prevent aspiration.

source.guideline: AGS feeding tubes in advanced dementia
source.recommendation: Feeding tubes in advanced dementia do not improve survival or prevent aspiration. Hand feeding is preferred.

diagram.alt: Text card. A tube does not stop aspiration and does not lengthen life here.

front: A patient with metastatic cancer that has stopped responding wants to know whether another round of chemotherapy is the only choice.
bottom: Name the prognosis, and offer care that is aimed at comfort.

bullets.clue: Hospice is for a prognosis of about six months if the disease runs its usual course, and it forgoes disease-directed treatment.
bullets.treat: Palliative care can start earlier, alongside treatment. Hospice is the choice when disease-directed treatment is no longer the goal.
bullets.trap: Offering another regimen without saying what it can and cannot do.

source.recommendation: Hospice requires a limited prognosis and a goal of comfort. Palliative care is broader and can accompany disease treatment.

diagram.alt: Text card. Name the prognosis, and offer care that is aimed at comfort.

front: A patient goes home after a heart-failure admission on a Friday. The next lab and visit are booked for six weeks.
bottom: See them within seven days.

bullets.clue: The week after discharge is when weight, kidneys, and potassium go wrong.
bullets.treat: A visit or a structured call within seven days, daily weights, and the medicines continued unless a number forces a hold.
bullets.trap: A six-week primary care visit as the only follow-up.

source.recommendation: Heart-failure discharge includes early follow-up, within about seven days, because that is when decompensation recurs.

diagram.alt: Text card. See them within seven days.

front: A patient on an ACE inhibitor develops a dry cough and the medicine is stopped. Nothing replaces it. The ejection fraction is 30 percent.
bottom: Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker. Do not leave the pathway untreated.

bullets.clue: The cough is a reason to change the drug, not a reason to abandon afterload reduction.
bullets.treat: An angiotensin receptor blocker, or an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor when that is the right next step.
bullets.trap: Stopping the class and substituting nothing.

source.recommendation: ACE-inhibitor cough is managed by switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker, not by stopping neurohormonal blockade.

diagram.alt: Text card. Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker. Do not leave the pathway untreated.

front: Spironolactone was started last month. Today's potassium is 5.6 and the creatinine has risen sharply.
bottom: Hold the drug and recheck. Do not refill the same dose.

bullets.clue: A small creatinine rise after an ACE inhibitor can be tolerated. A potassium of 5.6 on spironolactone is not.
bullets.treat: Stop or reduce the mineralocorticoid antagonist, review salt substitutes and kidney function, and recheck soon.
bullets.trap: Continuing the same dose because the patient feels well.

source.recommendation: Mineralocorticoid antagonists are stopped or reduced for significant hyperkalemia. Symptoms are a late clue.

diagram.alt: Text card. Hold the drug and recheck. Do not refill the same dose.

front: New atrial fibrillation is found on a routine exam. The patient feels fine, the pressure is normal, and the rate is 110.
bottom: Do not cardiovert this afternoon.

bullets.clue: Elective cardioversion needs a plan for thrombus: three weeks of anticoagulation or a clear transesophageal echo, then anticoagulation after.
bullets.treat: Control the rate, decide on stroke prevention, and get an echocardiogram. Cardioversion is a scheduled plan, not a same-hour convenience.
bullets.trap: A same-day shock in clinic because the patient is stable and busy.

source.recommendation: Stable new atrial fibrillation is not cardioverted without a thrombus plan. Rate control and stroke prevention come first.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not cardiovert this afternoon.

front: A 72-year-old loses consciousness while sitting and talking. There was no warning. A monitor later shows a long pause.
bottom: This syncope is cardiac. Do not send the patient home with a hydration sheet.

bullets.clue: No prodrome, occurrence while seated, and a pause are high-risk features.
bullets.treat: Monitor and refer for the conduction problem. Vasovagal syncope has a trigger and a warning.
bullets.trap: Oral fluids and primary care next month.

source.recommendation: Syncope while seated, without a prodrome, or with a documented pause is cardiac until proven otherwise.

diagram.alt: Text card. This syncope is cardiac. Do not send the patient home with a hydration sheet.

front: An anticoagulated patient hits their head, is awake, and has a normal neurologic exam in triage.
bottom: Image the head now, and watch afterward.

bullets.clue: A normal exam does not exclude a bleed that declares itself hours later.
bullets.treat: CT, a period of observation, and a plan to return. Do not discharge from triage.
bullets.trap: Reassurance and a ride home because the patient is talking.

source.guideline: ACEP mild traumatic brain injury guideline
source.recommendation: Anticoagulated patients with head trauma are imaged even when the exam is normal, and delayed bleeding is anticipated.

diagram.alt: Text card. Image the head now, and watch afterward.

front: A patient on amiodarone develops tremor and weight loss. The thyroid was not checked when the drug was started.
bottom: Check the thyroid. Amiodarone can push it either way.

bullets.clue: The drug blocks conversion and also loads the gland with iodine, so both low and high thyroid states occur.
bullets.treat: A TSH now, and a TSH before the next patient starts the drug. Treat the thyroid disorder you find.
bullets.trap: A beta blocker for the tremor and no thyroid test.

source.recommendation: Amiodarone causes both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism. TSH is checked before treatment and during it.

diagram.alt: Steps. Check the thyroid. Amiodarone can push it either way.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: medication use
front: A patient on digoxin is prescribed clarithromycin for a respiratory infection. Three days later they are nauseated and seeing yellow.
bottom: The antibiotic raised the digoxin level.

bullets.clue: Clarithromycin and some other drugs reduce digoxin clearance.
bullets.treat: Stop the interacting antibiotic, check the level, and treat toxicity if it is present.
bullets.trap: A second antibiotic from the same interacting class and a higher digoxin dose for the nausea.

source.recommendation: Macrolides such as clarithromycin can raise digoxin levels into the toxic range.

diagram.alt: Text card. The antibiotic raised the digoxin level.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: medication use
front: A patient on lithium starts a thiazide for blood pressure and a week later is confused and shaky.
bottom: The diuretic raised the lithium.

bullets.clue: Thiazides and nonsteroidal drugs both raise lithium. Dehydration does the same.
bullets.treat: Check the level, hold the lithium, hydrate, and pick a different blood pressure drug.
bullets.trap: Adding a nonsteroidal drug on top for the headache of toxicity.

source.recommendation: Thiazides and NSAIDs raise lithium levels. A new prescription is a reason to recheck the level.

diagram.alt: Text card. The diuretic raised the lithium.

front: Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 25. Metformin is still on the list at full dose.
bottom: Stop the metformin.

bullets.clue: Below 30 the drug is contraindicated because lactic acidosis becomes a real risk if the drug accumulates.
bullets.treat: Stop it under 30. Do not start it under 45. Between 30 and 45, if it is already in use, the dose is reduced and the kidney is watched.
bullets.trap: A full dose at a filtration rate of 25 because the A1c is good.

source.recommendation: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and is not started below 45.

diagram.alt: Text card. Stop the metformin.

front: A patient with longstanding diabetes has an A1c of 6.2 and describes sweating and confusion at 3 in the morning several nights a week.
bottom: Loosen the target. The nights are dangerous.

bullets.clue: A low A1c with hypoglycemia unawareness is harm, not success.
bullets.treat: Reduce the insulin that covers the night and set a higher target. Ask about driving.
bullets.trap: Congratulating the A1c and refilling the same doses.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
source.recommendation: Nocturnal hypoglycemia with a very low A1c means the goal is too tight and the regimen should be relaxed.

diagram.alt: Text card. Loosen the target. The nights are dangerous.

front: A patient with type 1 diabetes has a fever and is not hungry. A family member stopped the basal insulin because the patient was not eating.
bottom: Restart the basal insulin and check for ketones.

bullets.clue: Illness raises insulin need. Fasting does not remove it in type 1 diabetes.
bullets.treat: Sick-day rules: fluids, frequent glucose and ketone checks, basal insulin on board, and a threshold to be seen.
bullets.trap: Holding all insulin until the appetite returns.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
source.recommendation: Sick-day rules for type 1 diabetes keep basal insulin running and add ketone checks.

diagram.alt: Text card. Restart the basal insulin and check for ketones.

front: A five-day prednisone burst is planned for asthma. The family asks whether this means a lifelong diabetes pill, because last time the glucose hit 220.
bottom: Expect a temporary rise. Do not start a lifelong sulfonylurea for five days.

bullets.clue: Steroids raise glucose while they are present. The rise ends when the burst ends in a patient without diabetes.
bullets.treat: A short monitoring plan. A patient who already has diabetes may need a temporary insulin adjustment.
bullets.trap: A new chronic diabetes medicine for a five-day steroid.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
source.recommendation: Short glucocorticoid bursts raise glucose temporarily. They are not an indication for a new chronic oral diabetes drug.

diagram.alt: Text card. Expect a temporary rise. Do not start a lifelong sulfonylurea for five days.

front: Kidney disease is established, the A1c is 6.9, and the patient is not on a drug that protects the kidney.
bottom: Add a kidney-outcome drug even though the A1c is close to goal.

bullets.clue: An SGLT2 inhibitor slows kidney disease independent of how much it moves the A1c.
bullets.treat: Start the kidney-protective agent unless it is unsafe, and keep the A1c conversation separate.
bullets.trap: Withholding the drug because the A1c does not need help.

source.guideline: ADA and KDIGO diabetes in chronic kidney disease
source.recommendation: SGLT2 inhibitors are used for kidney protection in diabetic kidney disease, not only for glucose lowering.

diagram.alt: Text card. Add a kidney-outcome drug even though the A1c is close to goal.

front: An 80-year-old feels well. TSH is 6.2 on two checks, free hormone is normal, and antibodies are negative.
bottom: Do not start a full replacement dose for this number.

bullets.clue: Treat a TSH of 10 or more. A mild rise in an asymptomatic older adult is watched.
bullets.treat: Recheck and explain. A young patient who is pregnant or trying to conceive is a different threshold.
bullets.trap: A full weight-based dose of levothyroxine for a TSH of 6 in an older adult.

source.recommendation: Asymptomatic older adults with TSH below 10 are often observed. Treatment is usual once TSH is 10 or higher.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not start a full replacement dose for this number.

front: A frail 78-year-old has a TSH of 24 and needs levothyroxine. The calculated full replacement would be about 110 micrograms.
bottom: Start low, near 25 micrograms, and titrate.

bullets.clue: Full replacement is for young healthy adults. Older and cardiac patients are started low.
bullets.treat: A low starting dose, repeat TSH in six to eight weeks, and a slow climb.
bullets.trap: The full calculated dose on day one.

source.recommendation: Older adults and patients with heart disease start levothyroxine at a low dose, often about 25 micrograms.

diagram.alt: Text card. Start low, near 25 micrograms, and titrate.

front: Two weeks after a statin increase the patient has severe muscle pain. Creatine kinase is 2,400. Another patient has no pain and a kinase of 280.
bottom: Stop the statin in the patient who hurts. Do not stop it for a trivial enzyme bump.

bullets.clue: Symptoms plus a clearly high kinase mean stop. A small asymptomatic rise does not.
bullets.treat: Stop, hydrate if the kinase is very high, and revisit a statin later at a lower dose or a different drug.
bullets.trap: Stopping every statin forever because one kinase was slightly above the reference range.

source.recommendation: Statin muscle symptoms with a substantially elevated creatine kinase require stopping the drug. Asymptomatic mild elevations do not.

diagram.alt: Text card. Stop the statin in the patient who hurts. Do not stop it for a trivial enzyme bump.

front: A patient has taken a statin for a year with no muscle symptoms. A baseline liver panel was normal. An annual liver panel is ordered out of habit.
bottom: Do not order routine liver tests in an asymptomatic patient.

bullets.clue: Check enzymes if symptoms suggest liver injury. Do not schedule them yearly without a reason.
bullets.treat: Leave the statin. Test the liver if jaundice, severe fatigue, or pain appears.
bullets.trap: A yearly liver panel as a condition of the refill.

source.recommendation: After a normal baseline, routine monitoring of liver enzymes on a statin is not recommended in asymptomatic patients.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not order routine liver tests in an asymptomatic patient.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: medication use
front: A hospital proton-pump inhibitor is still being refilled three months after discharge. The patient never had a bleed, an ulcer, or reflux.
bottom: Stop it and ask why it was started.

bullets.clue: Many inpatient acid-suppression orders have no outpatient indication.
bullets.treat: Deprescribe and warn about rebound heartburn for a few days. Continue only if there is a real indication.
bullets.trap: A permanent refill because it was on the discharge list.

source.recommendation: Proton-pump inhibitors without an ongoing indication should be stopped. Discharge lists are not indications.

diagram.alt: Text card. Stop it and ask why it was started.

front: A patient with heart failure needs a colonoscopy. The prep offered is a sodium phosphate bottle.
bottom: Use a polyethylene glycol prep. Phosphate can injure the kidney.

bullets.clue: Phosphate preps cause phosphate nephropathy, especially in older patients and those with kidney disease or heart failure.
bullets.treat: A large-volume polyethylene glycol prep, with attention to the heart-failure volume.
bullets.trap: A phosphate prep because it is smaller and more convenient.

source.guideline: FDA sodium phosphate bowel prep warning
source.recommendation: Sodium phosphate bowel preparations can cause acute phosphate nephropathy and are a poor choice in heart failure and kidney disease.

diagram.alt: Text card. Use a polyethylene glycol prep. Phosphate can injure the kidney.

front: A screening stool test is positive. The hemoglobin is a little low. Iron is started and a blood count is planned in a month. No scope is booked.
bottom: The positive screen still needs a colonoscopy.

bullets.clue: Iron can fix the number and hide the cancer that the screen was meant to find.
bullets.treat: Schedule the colonoscopy. Iron can accompany it. Iron does not replace it.
bullets.trap: Rechecking the blood count after iron and calling the screen resolved.

source.recommendation: A positive fecal immunochemical test requires colonoscopy. Treating iron deficiency does not complete the evaluation.

diagram.alt: Text card. The positive screen still needs a colonoscopy.

front: A patient leaves after a chronic obstructive exacerbation and can walk only across the room. No rehabilitation is offered.
bottom: Refer to pulmonary rehabilitation after the hospitalization.

bullets.clue: Rehabilitation after an exacerbation reduces the chance of coming back and improves walking.
bullets.treat: A referral, inhaler teaching, and a follow-up. The five-day steroid course is already the right length. Do not stretch it to two weeks by habit.
bullets.trap: A refill of the rescue inhaler as the whole discharge plan.

source.recommendation: Pulmonary rehabilitation is indicated after a COPD hospitalization. Steroid bursts for exacerbations are about five days.

diagram.alt: Text card. Refer to pulmonary rehabilitation after the hospitalization.

front: A 30-year-old is well six weeks after an ordinary pneumonia. A routine follow-up chest film is scheduled because that is the clinic habit.
bottom: A recovered young nonsmoker does not need the film.

bullets.clue: Follow-up imaging is for symptoms that persist or for a smoking and age risk of cancer.
bullets.treat: Skip the film when recovery is complete and cancer risk is low. Order it when symptoms remain or the smoking history demands it.
bullets.trap: A film for every pneumonia at six weeks.

source.recommendation: Routine follow-up radiographs after pneumonia are not required when the patient has recovered and cancer is unlikely.

diagram.alt: Text card. A recovered young nonsmoker does not need the film.

front: A patient uses a rescue inhaler every day and wakes at night twice a week. The only refill request is for the rescue inhaler.
bottom: Add an inhaled corticosteroid. A rescue inhaler is not a controller.

bullets.clue: Daily rescue use means the airway inflammation is untreated.
bullets.treat: Start an inhaled corticosteroid, teach the device, and review triggers. Do not refill albuterol alone.
bullets.trap: Another rescue inhaler and a visit in six months.

source.recommendation: Frequent rescue use means the patient needs an inhaled corticosteroid. Reliever-only care is not appropriate.

diagram.alt: Text card. Add an inhaled corticosteroid. A rescue inhaler is not a controller.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: population health
front: A patient who smokes is told to quit and handed a pamphlet. No medicine and no follow-up are offered.
bottom: Combine counseling with a medicine. A pamphlet is not the treatment.

bullets.clue: Varenicline, nicotine replacement, or bupropion plus counseling beats advice alone.
bullets.treat: Offer a drug and at least a brief counseling plan, and arrange follow-up. The patient can decline.
bullets.trap: Advice alone recorded as cessation counseling.

source.recommendation: The USPSTF recommends behavioral counseling plus pharmacotherapy for tobacco cessation in adults.

diagram.alt: Text card. Combine counseling with a medicine. A pamphlet is not the treatment.

front: A patient drinks most days, has tried to cut down, and is annoyed by questions about it. Liver tests are only mildly off. They want help.
bottom: Offer naltrexone or acamprosate, not disulfiram as a casual first drug.

bullets.clue: A short screen that is positive deserves a treatment offer, not a lecture.
bullets.treat: Naltrexone if opioids are absent and the liver allows it, or acamprosate. Add counseling.
bullets.trap: Disulfiram on the first visit because it sounds decisive.

source.recommendation: Naltrexone and acamprosate are first-line medications for alcohol use disorder. Disulfiram is not the casual first choice.

diagram.alt: Text card. Offer naltrexone or acamprosate, not disulfiram as a casual first drug.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: medication use
front: Acute back pain with no red flags. A long-acting opioid is offered as the first prescription.
bottom: Do not start a long-acting opioid for acute pain.

bullets.clue: If an opioid is truly needed, it is immediate release, at a low dose, for a short time, with naloxone in the house.
bullets.treat: Stay active, use nonopioid treatments first, and check the prescription database before any opioid.
bullets.trap: A fentanyl patch for a three-day strain.

source.recommendation: Acute pain is not treated with a long-acting opioid. Nonopioid care comes first, and any opioid is short and immediate release.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not start a long-acting opioid for acute pain.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: medication use
front: An older adult has taken a benzodiazepine every night for eight years and is asked to stop it tomorrow because it is on a warning list.
bottom: Taper over weeks to months. Do not stop tomorrow.

bullets.clue: An abrupt stop can cause withdrawal seizures. The goal is still to come off.
bullets.treat: A slow taper, sleep counseling, and a warning about what withdrawal feels like.
bullets.trap: A cold stop on Monday because the drug is inappropriate.

source.recommendation: Chronic benzodiazepines in older adults should be tapered, not stopped abruptly.

diagram.alt: Text card. Taper over weeks to months. Do not stop tomorrow.

front: A patient has struggled to sleep for three months. The request is for a nightly controlled sleep drug.
bottom: Start with insomnia therapy, not a nightly controlled substance.

bullets.clue: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is the first-line treatment and outlasts a pill.
bullets.treat: Refer for that therapy. Use a drug only as a short bridge if you must, with an exit plan.
bullets.trap: A monthly refill of a Z-drug as the plan.

source.recommendation: Chronic insomnia is treated first with cognitive behavioral therapy, not with a standing hypnotic.

diagram.alt: Text card. Start with insomnia therapy, not a nightly controlled substance.

front: Three weeks after a spouse's death, a patient has waves of sadness, is eating with family, and has no wish to die. Self-worth is intact.
bottom: This is grief. Do not start an antidepressant at the funeral.

bullets.clue: Grief comes in waves and keeps self-worth. Depression is pervasive, with worthlessness and loss of function.
bullets.treat: Support and a planned revisit. Treat if function collapses, worthlessness appears, or the patient is unsafe.
bullets.trap: An antidepressant on day three of bereavement, or ignoring a patient who cannot function two months later.

source.recommendation: Ordinary grief is supported, not medicated at once. Depression is a different syndrome and is treated when it is present.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is grief. Do not start an antidepressant at the funeral.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: population health
front: A clinic screen for depression scores in the severe range. The patient has no plan for suicide. The next open therapy visit is in three months.
bottom: Do not leave a severe score for three months.

bullets.clue: A positive screen is an action, not a number to file.
bullets.treat: Same-week assessment, start treatment, and a safety check. Referral alone with a long wait is not enough.
bullets.trap: A pamphlet and a seasonal visit.

source.recommendation: Adults should be screened for depression when systems exist to treat it. A severe score needs prompt treatment, not a distant referral.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not leave a severe score for three months.

front: Acute low back pain for four days. No fever, no cancer history, no weakness, no bladder symptoms. An MRI and an opioid are ordered.
bottom: Neither is the first move.

bullets.clue: Red flags are missing. Imaging does not speed recovery and finds irrelevant changes.
bullets.treat: Stay active, use nonopioid pain care, and explain the course. Image if a red flag appears or the pain is not following the usual path.
bullets.trap: An MRI on day four and a long-acting opioid.

source.recommendation: Acute low back pain without red flags is treated with activity and nonopioid care. Routine early MRI is not indicated.

diagram.alt: Text card. Neither is the first move.

front: Knee pain for years, worse with stairs, no hot joint and no injury. The film shows joint-space loss. Surgery is the first offer.
bottom: Exercise and weight loss come before a replacement conversation.

bullets.clue: A topical anti-inflammatory is kinder to an older stomach than a standing oral one.
bullets.treat: A strengthening program, weight loss if needed, and a topical anti-inflammatory. Replacement is for function that remains unacceptable.
bullets.trap: Scheduling a replacement from the first film.

source.recommendation: Knee osteoarthritis starts with exercise, weight loss, and topical anti-inflammatory therapy. Replacement is later.

diagram.alt: Text card. Exercise and weight loss come before a replacement conversation.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: nervous system and special senses
front: Brief spinning only when rolling over in bed, lasting under a minute, with no hearing loss and no neurologic deficit.
bottom: This is loose crystal in the canal. Do the repositioning maneuver.

bullets.clue: The Dix-Hallpike test reproduces it. An Epley maneuver treats the common canal.
bullets.treat: Reposition the crystal. Do not order a head CT for a classic positional story.
bullets.trap: Meclizine for a month and a CT.

source.guideline: AAN benign paroxysmal positional vertigo guideline
source.recommendation: Brief positional vertigo is treated with a canalith repositioning maneuver. Imaging is not the first step.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is loose crystal in the canal. Do the repositioning maneuver.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: nervous system and special senses
front: Headache days have climbed past four a month and the patient is missing work. The only prescription is a triptan. The patient also has coronary disease.
bottom: Add prevention, and do not use a triptan in coronary disease.

bullets.clue: Frequent or disabling migraine deserves a preventive drug. Triptans constrict vessels.
bullets.treat: Start a preventive and choose an acute drug that is safe for the heart.
bullets.trap: A triptan refill as the whole plan in a patient with coronary disease.

source.recommendation: Frequent disabling migraine needs prevention. Triptans are avoided in coronary artery disease.

diagram.alt: Text card. Add prevention, and do not use a triptan in coronary disease.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: nervous system and special senses
front: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye. The retina is pale and the macula looks like a cherry-red spot.
bottom: Treat this as a stroke of the eye, today.

bullets.clue: A central retinal artery occlusion is an ischemic stroke equivalent.
bullets.treat: Emergency stroke evaluation, not an eye clinic next month.
bullets.trap: An outpatient ophthalmology appointment next week.

source.guideline: AHA scientific statement on retinal artery occlusion
source.recommendation: Central retinal artery occlusion is evaluated as a stroke equivalent in an emergency setting.

diagram.alt: Text card. Treat this as a stroke of the eye, today.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: nervous system and special senses
front: A red eye hurts, the pupil is small, and light makes the pain much worse. Vision is blurred.
bottom: This is not conjunctivitis. Same-day eye care.

bullets.clue: Pain, photophobia, and a small pupil suggest uveitis, ulcer, or acute glaucoma. Itch and discharge suggest conjunctivitis.
bullets.treat: Urgent ophthalmology. Do not send an antibiotic drop and a week of waiting.
bullets.trap: Erythromycin ointment for every red eye.

source.recommendation: A painful red eye with photophobia or blurred vision needs same-day ophthalmology, not routine conjunctivitis care.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is not conjunctivitis. Same-day eye care.

front: A 70-year-old breaks a hip after tripping on a rug. A density test has never been done. The discharge summary mentions the hardware and not the bone.
bottom: Treat the fragility fracture. Do not wait for a density score to call it osteoporosis.

bullets.clue: A hip fracture from standing height is the diagnosis of fragility.
bullets.treat: Start osteoporosis therapy and fall prevention around the admission. A density test can refine the choice. It should not delay the recognition.
bullets.trap: A plan to discuss the bone at the annual visit next year.

source.recommendation: A fragility hip fracture is treated as osteoporosis. Waiting a year for a density test misses the indication.

diagram.alt: Text card. Treat the fragility fracture. Do not wait for a density score to call it osteoporosis.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: female reproductive system
front: A 32-year-old with migraine that includes aura asks for a combined estrogen pill.
bottom: Do not use estrogen. The aura is the contraindication.

bullets.clue: Aura plus estrogen raises stroke risk. A progestin-only method or a nonhormonal method is appropriate.
bullets.treat: Offer a progestin-only pill, an implant, an injection, or a device. Document the aura.
bullets.trap: A combined pill because the migraines are infrequent.

source.guideline: CDC Medical Eligibility Criteria for contraception
source.recommendation: Migraine with aura is a contraindication to combined hormonal contraception because of stroke risk.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not use estrogen. The aura is the contraindication.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: female reproductive system
front: Unprotected intercourse was four days ago. The patient wants to prevent a pregnancy and was told it is too late for anything.
bottom: It is not too late for every method.

bullets.clue: A copper intrauterine device is the most effective option and works later than the pills. Ulipristal reaches further than levonorgestrel.
bullets.treat: Offer the method that still fits the interval, ideally the device if the patient wants it.
bullets.trap: Sending the patient away at 96 hours with no options.

source.recommendation: Emergency contraception options depend on the interval. A copper IUD remains effective later than oral levonorgestrel.

diagram.alt: Text card. It is not too late for every method.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: pregnancy, childbirth, and the puerperium
front: A patient had a negative HIV and syphilis test in a prior pregnancy three years ago. This is a new pregnancy. No labs are drawn because the old ones were fine.
bottom: Test again. Every pregnancy is tested.

bullets.clue: Incidence during the interval is the point of repeating the tests.
bullets.treat: HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, blood type, and antibody screen in this pregnancy.
bullets.trap: Carrying forward a three-year-old negative result.

source.guideline: CDC and ACOG prenatal laboratory guidance
source.recommendation: HIV and syphilis testing are recommended in every pregnancy, not only the first one.

diagram.alt: Text card. Test again. Every pregnancy is tested.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: pregnancy, childbirth, and the puerperium
front: A patient delivers and wants an intrauterine device. She is told to wait six weeks even though the delivery was uncomplicated and there is no infection.
bottom: It can be placed before she leaves, if she wants that.

bullets.clue: Immediate postpartum placement is safe and prevents the gap when contraception is missing.
bullets.treat: Offer immediate placement or a planned interval placement. Do not invent a mandatory six-week wait.
bullets.trap: A blanket six-week delay.

source.recommendation: An intrauterine device may be placed immediately after birth when infection and other contraindications are absent.

diagram.alt: Text card. It can be placed before she leaves, if she wants that.

task_area: Advanced clinical medicine: female reproductive system
front: A breastfeeding patient has a tender, red, wedge-shaped area on one breast and a fever. She is told to stop nursing on that side until the antibiotic is done.
bottom: Keep emptying the breast, including by nursing.

bullets.clue: Stopping leads to a worse obstruction. An antibiotic is added when infection is present. The infant can keep feeding.
bullets.treat: Effective milk removal, rest, and an antibiotic compatible with nursing if there are infectious signs.
bullets.trap: Binding the breast and discarding the milk.

source.guideline: Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine mastitis protocol
source.recommendation: Mastitis is treated with continued milk removal. Nursing does not stop.

diagram.alt: Text card. Keep emptying the breast, including by nursing.

front: A 3-day-old is yellow, feeding well, and otherwise normal. The bilirubin number is handed to you without the age in hours.
bottom: Plot it against hours of age. A bare number is not a decision.

bullets.clue: Treatment lines depend on age in hours and gestational age. A 3-day-old is not a 3-hour-old.
bullets.treat: Use the hour-specific threshold. Feed frequently and recheck. Do not jump to exchange transfusion for a number below the line.
bullets.trap: Treating every bilirubin over 10 the same way.

source.recommendation: Phototherapy thresholds are hour-specific and gestation-specific. A bilirubin value without age cannot be interpreted.

diagram.alt: Text card. Plot it against hours of age. A bare number is not a decision.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: population health
front: A newborn screen is reported as positive for a metabolic disease. The infant looks well. The family is about to be told the child has the disease.
bottom: A positive screen is not a diagnosis.

bullets.clue: Screens are set to be sensitive. Confirmatory testing decides.
bullets.treat: Tell the family it is a screen, expedite the confirmatory test, and do not label the child yet.
bullets.trap: A definitive diagnosis from the screening card.

source.recommendation: Newborn screening positives require confirmatory testing. They are not diagnoses.

diagram.alt: Text card. A positive screen is not a diagnosis.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: population health
front: An 18-month-old is in clinic for a viral cold. No developmental screen has been done at this visit or the last.
bottom: Screen development at 18 months, including autism, even though the visit was for a cold.

bullets.clue: The 18-month and 24-month visits are the autism-screening points.
bullets.treat: Do the screen at this visit or book it within days. A cold is not a reason to skip it for a year.
bullets.trap: Waiting until kindergarten.

source.recommendation: Autism-specific screening is recommended at 18 and 24 months, including at visits that start with another complaint.

diagram.alt: Text card. Screen development at 18 months, including autism, even though the visit was for a cold.

front: A 7-year-old is fidgety in the office. A stimulant is prescribed at the first visit. No teacher report and no home criteria are documented.
bottom: Do not start a stimulant on one observation.

bullets.clue: The diagnosis needs symptoms in more than one setting, impairment, and the criteria. The office snapshot is not that.
bullets.treat: Collect home and school reports, rule out sleep and learning problems, and then decide.
bullets.trap: A stimulant because the child would not sit still for the exam.

source.recommendation: ADHD is diagnosed from criteria across more than one setting. A single office observation is not enough to start a stimulant.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not start a stimulant on one observation.

front: A 16-year-old is seen with a parent for a sports form. The whole interview happens with the parent in the room, including questions about sex and substances.
bottom: Spend part of the visit with the adolescent alone.

bullets.clue: Confidential care for sensitive services is what makes the history true. Safety issues are still shared.
bullets.treat: Ask the parent to step out for a portion. Explain what will and will not be kept private.
bullets.trap: A complete interview conducted only in front of the parent.

source.recommendation: Adolescents should be interviewed alone for part of each visit so sensitive care can be delivered safely.

diagram.alt: Text card. Spend part of the visit with the adolescent alone.

front: A child has a fever and a rash that does not blanch. They are limp and cold at the edges.
bottom: Treat meningococcal disease now. Do not wait for the rash to look classic.

bullets.clue: Non-blanching rash plus toxicity is enough. The lumbar puncture must not delay the antibiotic.
bullets.treat: Antibiotics, resuscitation, and then the confirmatory studies.
bullets.trap: A viral-illness handout for a non-blanching rash in a toxic child.

source.recommendation: Fever, a non-blanching rash, and toxicity are treated immediately as invasive meningococcal disease.

diagram.alt: Steps. Treat meningococcal disease now. Do not wait for the rash to look classic.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: systems-based practice
front: A colleague is seeing patients while visibly impaired. The schedule is full, and covering the impairment would keep the clinic moving.
bottom: Act to protect the patients. Do not quietly cover the shift.

bullets.clue: The duty is to the patients in front of an impaired colleague, and to a process that gets the colleague help.
bullets.treat: Remove them from patient care and report through the institutional path.
bullets.trap: Seeing their patients for them and telling no one.

source.guideline: AMA Code of Medical Ethics on physician impairment
source.recommendation: Physicians must intervene when a colleague's impairment threatens patients. Quiet coverage is not the duty.

diagram.alt: Text card. Act to protect the patients. Do not quietly cover the shift.

front: A patient asks you to sign a disability form stating they cannot work, when your exam and the records show they can.
bottom: Decline. The form has to be true.

bullets.clue: Advocacy does not include a false statement. You can describe what you actually found.
bullets.treat: Explain what you can certify, offer appropriate care, and do not sign a statement you know is false.
bullets.trap: Signing so the patient will not be upset.

source.guideline: AMA Code of Medical Ethics on honesty
source.recommendation: Physicians do not certify facts they know to be false, including disability statements.

diagram.alt: Text card. Decline. The form has to be true.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: medication use
front: An older adult takes an SSRI and asks for a standing nonsteroidal drug for osteoarthritis. They have already had one stomach bleed.
bottom: Do not add that combination.

bullets.clue: Age, an SSRI, a prior bleed, and a nonsteroidal drug multiply the bleeding risk.
bullets.treat: Use a topical anti-inflammatory, acetaminophen, or another plan. If a nonsteroidal drug is unavoidable, protect the stomach and limit the time.
bullets.trap: Ibuprofen around the clock on top of the SSRI after a prior bleed.

source.recommendation: Nonsteroidal drugs plus SSRIs in older adults raise gastrointestinal bleeding risk, especially after a prior bleed.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not add that combination.

front: Ten days after a coronary stent the patient wants both antiplatelet drugs stopped for a dental cleaning.
bottom: Do not stop both. The stent is young.

bullets.clue: Aspirin continues. Elective procedures wait until the minimum dual-therapy window has passed. A cleaning rarely needs both drugs off.
bullets.treat: Talk to cardiology before any interruption. Continue aspirin.
bullets.trap: Holding aspirin and the P2Y12 inhibitor on day 10.

source.recommendation: Dual antiplatelet therapy is not stopped in the early weeks after a stent for a routine dental cleaning.

diagram.alt: Text card. Do not stop both. The stent is young.

front: The INR is 12. The patient feels well, the gums are not bleeding, and there is no head injury.
bottom: Hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K. Do not transfuse plasma for a number.

bullets.clue: Plasma is for serious bleeding. A high INR without bleeding is reversed more gently.
bullets.treat: Oral vitamin K and a recheck. Resume warfarin at a lower dose when the INR is back in range.
bullets.trap: Fresh frozen plasma because the INR looks extreme and the patient feels fine.

source.recommendation: For an INR above 10 without bleeding, oral vitamin K is suggested. Plasma is reserved for major bleeding.

diagram.alt: Text card. Hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K. Do not transfuse plasma for a number.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: medication use
front: A patient on a twice-daily direct oral anticoagulant remembers the morning dose at dinner time, an hour before the evening dose.
bottom: Skip the missed morning dose. Do not double up.

bullets.clue: If the miss is noticed well before the next dose, it can be taken. Close to the next dose, skip it.
bullets.treat: Take the evening dose on time. Never take two doses at once to catch up.
bullets.trap: Two tablets tonight to make up the morning.

source.guideline: ACC expert consensus on direct oral anticoagulants
source.recommendation: A missed direct oral anticoagulant dose is taken when remembered unless it is close to the next dose. Doses are not doubled.

diagram.alt: Text card. Skip the missed morning dose. Do not double up.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: perioperative care
front: An ACE inhibitor for uncomplicated hypertension is written as take on the morning of surgery with a sip of water.
bottom: Hold it that morning.

bullets.clue: These drugs raise the chance of low pressure after induction. A beta blocker the patient already takes is the drug you continue.
bullets.treat: Hold the ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker the morning of surgery unless heart failure makes the team decide otherwise.
bullets.trap: Giving every blood pressure pill on the morning of surgery, including the ACE inhibitor.

source.recommendation: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are often held the morning of surgery because of intraoperative hypotension.

diagram.alt: Text card. Hold it that morning.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: population health
front: A healthy 52-year-old has never received a pneumococcal vaccine and is in clinic for a blood pressure check.
bottom: Give a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine. Fifty is the age.

bullets.clue: The adult schedule lowered the routine age to 50. A visit for something else is still a vaccine visit.
bullets.treat: One conjugate vaccine per the current schedule, and document it. Do not wait for the 65th birthday.
bullets.trap: Telling the patient to come back at 65.

source.recommendation: ACIP recommends a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine for adults 50 and older. Confirm the current schedule before the feed is shown to students.

diagram.alt: Text card. Give a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine. Fifty is the age.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: population health
front: A patient with hives after eating eggs asks whether they can receive the influenza vaccine.
bottom: Yes. Egg allergy is not a contraindication.

bullets.clue: Any age-appropriate influenza vaccine can be used. A history of hives, or even a more severe egg reaction, is not a reason to skip it.
bullets.treat: Vaccinate with the usual vaccine and observe as you would any patient. The only refusal is a severe reaction to a prior dose of the vaccine itself.
bullets.trap: Sending the patient away every autumn because of an egg allergy.

source.recommendation: Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination.

diagram.alt: Text card. Yes. Egg allergy is not a contraindication.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: systems-based practice
front: A patient had a seizure yesterday. They ask if they may drive to work tomorrow and whether you will keep the seizure off any report.
bottom: They may not drive. Follow your state's reporting rule.

bullets.clue: The seizure-free interval is set by the state. Some states require the physician to report. Some put the duty on the driver.
bullets.treat: Tell the patient not to drive, document the advice, and report if your state requires it. Do not promise secrecy you cannot keep.
bullets.trap: A private suggestion to be careful, with no mention of the law.

source.recommendation: After a seizure the patient does not drive until the legal seizure-free interval is met, and state reporting rules are followed.

diagram.alt: Text card. They may not drive. Follow your state's reporting rule.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: systems-based practice
front: An older adult has bruises in different stages and flinches when the caregiver is asked to step out. The caregiver says the patient falls a lot.
bottom: Report suspected abuse. Do not investigate it yourself first.

bullets.clue: A vulnerable adult with an inconsistent story is reported to adult protective services.
bullets.treat: Make the report, treat the injuries, and document the findings. You do not need proof.
bullets.trap: Waiting until you are sure, or confronting the caregiver as your only action.

source.guideline: Elder Justice and APS reporting standards
source.recommendation: Suspected abuse of a vulnerable adult is reported. Certainty is not required.

diagram.alt: Text card. Report suspected abuse. Do not investigate it yourself first.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: systems-based practice
front: A toddler has a spiral fracture of the femur. The story is that the child rolled off a couch. The exam shows older bruises the story does not explain.
bottom: Report suspected abuse.

bullets.clue: The fracture and the story do not match, and there are older injuries.
bullets.treat: Treat the fracture, report to child protective services, and do not send the child home to the same unexplained risk.
bullets.trap: Accepting the couch story because spiral fractures can sometimes be accidental.

source.recommendation: Injuries that do not match the developmental story, especially with older unexplained bruises, are reported as suspected abuse.

diagram.alt: Text card. Report suspected abuse.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: perioperative care
front: A person who can become pregnant is scheduled for elective surgery next week. The last menstrual period is not in the chart. No pregnancy test is ordered.
bottom: Test before the operation.

bullets.clue: Elective surgery and anesthesia in an unrecognized pregnancy are avoidable.
bullets.treat: A pregnancy test after consent, or a documented reason it was declined. Do not discover the pregnancy in the operating room.
bullets.trap: Proceeding because the patient says they are probably not pregnant.

source.recommendation: Patients who could be pregnant are offered pregnancy testing before elective anesthesia.

diagram.alt: Text card. Test before the operation.

task_area: Foundations of independent practice: perioperative care
front: A patient with known obstructive sleep apnea is coming for surgery. Their machine is at home. The recovery order says oxygen by nasal cannula only.
bottom: Bring the machine and use it after surgery.

bullets.clue: The danger is the hours after anesthesia, when sedatives and opioids meet an untreated airway.
bullets.treat: Have the patient bring their device, use it in recovery, and limit the sedatives.
bullets.trap: Discovering the apnea after a desaturation in the recovery room.

source.guideline: ASA obstructive sleep apnea perioperative guideline
source.recommendation: Patients with obstructive sleep apnea should use their positive-airway-pressure device in the perioperative period.

diagram.alt: Text card. Bring the machine and use it after surgery.
